analysis.summary:
This 31-year-old male presents with a four-day acute episode of episodic chest tightness, palpitations, and shortness of breath—cardinal symptoms of cardiac qi insufficiency—layered over a chronic foundation of fatigue and low spirit. His weak pulse, the cornerstone of palpation findings, confirms that his heart lacks the qi strength to generate normal circulatory force. The red tongue with thin coating is crucial: it tells us that alongside qi deficiency, yin reserves are depleted and heat is emerging from that depletion; a chronically stressed or overworked body consumes both qi and yin, leaving only heat behind. The bilateral lower-leg swelling indicates that his spleen qi—dependent on heart qi support—cannot transform and move fluids as it should, allowing them to pool in the lower body; this is not heart failure in the biomedical sense, but a qi-transformation failure.

The pattern integrates four key findings: (1) palpitations and chest tightness point directly to the heart's qi insufficiency; (2) shortness of breath reflects the lung's lack of qi support and the heart's inability to push blood into pulmonary circulation; (3) fatigue and low spirit are the textbook face of qi deficiency affecting both body and shen; (4) the edema, combined with the weak spleen function implied by fatigue, shows fluid accumulating because the qi pump is failing to move it. His constitution—qi-deficient—explains why even four days of acute stress triggered this crisis: his reservoir was always low.

The red tongue is a warning that chronic depletion has begun to heat: yin has been consumed, and the body's thermostat is drifting upward. If left untreated, this patient will slide toward yin-deficiency heat disorders, insomnia, and worsening cardiac insufficiency. However, the acute presentation also demands biomedical exclusion: a new-onset chest tightness with dyspnea lasting four days is a cardiac emergency until proven otherwise. TCM diagnosis coexists with—not replaces—urgent evaluation for acute myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, or arrhythmia.

Treatment must operate on two tracks: immediate biomedical screening to rule out structural or acute cardiac pathology, and TCM restoration of heart and spleen qi to reverse the underlying deficiency. The prognosis is good if the acute phase is medically cleared: qi-deficiency patterns respond well to tonification, and younger patients typically recover qi reserves within weeks to months with proper treatment, rest, and dietary support.

Calms palpitations, settles the spirit in the heart, and supports yin regeneration—critical for low spirit and insomnia accompanying this pattern.

ST36 Zusanli (足三里, Leg Three Miles) — located 3 cun below ST35 (Dubi, the lateral border of the patella when knee is bent), one finger-width lateral to the anterior tibial crest (the bony ridge on the front of the shin). Gentle circular massage for 1–2 minutes, once daily. The most important tonification point in TCM; directly tonifies spleen qi, supports heart qi, aids fluid metabolism, and builds stamina—addresses fatigue, edema, and qi insufficiency comprehensively.

PC8 Laogong (劳宫, Palace of Labor) — located in the palm at the center of the closed fist, between the 2nd and 3rd metacarpal bones (or at the tip of the middle finger when a fist is made). Gentle sustained pressure or light circular massage (20–30 rotations) on both hands, once daily. Calms the spirit, supports heart qi, and reduces palpitations; particularly useful in acute episodes.

BL15 Xinshu (心俞, Heart Shu) — located 1.5 cun lateral to the lower border of the spinous process of T5 (the 5th thoracic vertebra, roughly at the level of the bottom of the shoulder blade). Self-massage is difficult; instead, have a partner do gentle circular massage or apply a warming patch here. The back-shu point for the heart; directly strengthens heart qi and resolves palpitations.
exercise: Tai Chi or standing qigong (站桩, zhan zhuang) — 10–15 minutes, 4–5 times weekly. Focus on slow, controlled movements that synchronize breath with motion. Tai Chi gently moves qi and blood without depleting reserves, improves heart efficiency, and aids emotional regulation. Avoid vigorous or competitive exercise until edema resolves and palpitations cease.

Gentle walking (散步, san bu) — 20–30 minutes at a conversational pace, once daily. Walking supports spleen qi and fluid circulation without shock to the weak heart. If palpitations or dyspnea arise during walking, slow down or stop immediately.
recommendations.emotional_care: The low spirit and palpitations are intimately linked: the Heart houses the Shen (spirit/consciousness), and qi deficiency leaves the Shen unanchored, resulting in anxiety, palpitations, and depression. Emotional support is as important as herbs. Encourage the patient to reduce worry and perfectionism—excessive mental labor depletes heart yin and qi further. Suggest daily quiet time (10–15 min) for meditation, journaling, or simply sitting in nature to allow the spirit to settle. The patient should discuss with family or friends the need for reduced work expectations during recovery; guilt or self-pressure will sabotage healing. Consider that the 4-day acute episode may have been triggered by a stressful event; processing that event emotionally (talking it through, accepting it, letting go of blame) is part of recovery.

herbal_formulas.name: Four Gentlemen Decoction (Si Jun Zi Tang, 四君子汤) — Modified
ingredients: Ren Shen (人参, Ginseng root) — 6g [tonifies original Qi and Heart]
Bai Zhu (白术, Atractylodes macrocephala rhizome) — 9g [tonifies Spleen Qi, aids fluid transformation]
Fu Ling (茯苓, Poria sclerotium) — 9g [tonifies Spleen Qi, drains dampness and edema]
Zhi Gan Cao (炙甘草, honey-fried Licorice root) — 6g [tonifies Spleen and Heart Qi, harmonizes other herbs]
Da Zao (大枣, Chinese jujube fruit) — 3 pieces [tonifies Spleen and Heart Qi, calms spirit]
Gou Qi Zi (枸杞, Goji fruit) — 9g [nourishes Kidney Yin, supports Heart Yin regeneration to address the red tongue]
Dan Shen (丹参, Salvia miltiorrhiza root) — 9g [invigorates blood and calms spirit, prevents qi stagnation and supports yin nourishment]
herbal_formulas.dosage: Decoct herbs in 500 mL water, simmer 40 minutes, drink once daily in the afternoon or evening. Duration: 2–4 weeks, then reassess with practitioner.
herbal_formulas.purpose: This classical qi-tonifying formula is modified with goji berry and dan shen to address the concurrent yin deficiency and heat indicated by the red tongue. It directly restores heart and spleen qi, supports fluid transformation to resolve edema, and nourishes the spirit (shen). The formula is gentle and appropriate for a weak, recently-symptomatic patient.

herbal_formulas.name: Heavenly Emperor Tonifies the Heart Decoction (Tian Wang Bu Xin Dan, 天王补心丹) — *Optional second formula if insomnia or anxiety worsens*
ingredients: Suan Zao Ren (酸枣仁, Ziziphus jujuba var. spinosa seed) — 12g [calms spirit, anchors shen]
Mai Dong (麦冬, Ophiopogon japonicus tuber) — 9g [nourishes Heart and Lung Yin]
Tian Dong (天冬, Asparagus cochinchinensis tuber) — 9g [nourishes Lung and Kidney Yin]
Xuan Shen (玄参, Scrophularia ningpoensis root) — 9g [clears residual heat, nourishes Yin]
Sheng Di Huang (生地黄, uncooked Rehmannia root) — 9g [nourishes Yin and cools heat from deficiency]
herbal_formulas.dosage: Decoct as above; use if primary formula is well-tolerated but sleep remains poor or anxiety/palpitations worsen. Duration: 2–3 weeks.
herbal_formulas.purpose: This formula specifically addresses the heart yin deficiency and residual heat (the red tongue), calms a troubled spirit, and improves sleep quality. Use as a second or adjunct formula only after the primary tonification with Si Jun Zi Tang has begun showing benefit.

warning_signs: Sudden severe chest pain (crushing, radiating to arm or jaw) lasting more than 10 minutes — seek emergency room immediately; possible acute myocardial infarction
Syncope (fainting) or near-syncope (severe dizziness with loss of consciousness) — indicates possible arrhythmia or hemodynamic collapse; emergency evaluation required
Sudden severe dyspnea at rest, or dyspnea worsening despite rest — possible pulmonary embolism or acute heart failure; medical emergency
Palpitations accompanied by chest pain and sweating — red flag for acute cardiac event; emergency evaluation
Edema spreading rapidly to the face, throat, or causing severe restriction — possible angioedema or acute vascular compromise; urgent medical attention
contraindications: Do NOT discontinue any biomedically-prescribed cardiac medications (beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors, aspirin, etc.) without physician approval, even if TCM symptoms improve

Do NOT perform strenuous exercise, including gym workouts, running, or competitive sports, until palpitations have fully ceased and physician or TCM practitioner clears you; excessive exertion risks acute decompensation

Do NOT take stimulating supplements or energy drinks (especially those containing ephedrine, caffeine in high doses, or ginseng without professional guidance) — these overstimulate an already-fragile heart
precautions.special_notes: CRITICAL BIOMEDICAL EXCLUSION REQUIRED: This patient's 4-day acute onset of chest tightness with palpitations and dyspnea must be evaluated urgently by a cardiologist or emergency physician to rule out acute myocardial infarction, coronary artery disease, arrhythmia, pulmonary embolism, or acute heart failure. An ECG, troponin level, BNP or NT-proBNP (to assess for heart failure), chest X-ray, and possibly echocardiography are standard. TCM diagnosis of Heart Qi Deficiency coexists with and does not replace conventional cardiac evaluation. Only after serious structural or acute pathology has been excluded should the patient rely on TCM tonification as the primary treatment. The edema, while consistent with qi-deficiency patterns in TCM, must also be evaluated for causes such as hepatic disease, renal insufficiency, or venous insufficiency. The patient should also be screened for sleep apnea (which can present with nocturnal palpitations and daytime fatigue) and thyroid dysfunction (which can cause similar presentations). Once serious biomedical causes are ruled out, TCM offers excellent supportive care and genuine resolution of the underlying qi deficiency driving the symptoms.

follow_up.timeline: Reassess after 2 weeks of treatment (herbal formula + lifestyle modifications). If significant improvement in palpitations, edema, and fatigue is evident, continue treatment for an additional 2–4 weeks. If minimal change or worsening, return for pattern reassessment or consider additional biomedical investigation.
follow_up.expected_improvement: Week 1–2: Reduction in frequency or severity of palpitations; possible early improvement in sleep quality and low spirit. Week 2–3: Noticeable decrease in edema, improved energy for daily activities, fatigue less pronounced after light exertion. Week 3–4: Palpitations largely resolved, edema significantly diminished or absent, spirit lifted, able to resume light work without triggering symptoms. Full recovery of qi reserves (and prevention of relapse) typically requires 4–8 weeks of consistent treatment and lifestyle adherence.
follow_up.next_steps: 1) Obtain urgent biomedical clearance (ECG, troponin, echo if indicated) before starting intensive TCM treatment. 2) Once cleared, begin Si Jun Zi Tang modified formula immediately alongside lifestyle modifications. 3) Schedule follow-up with TCM practitioner in 2 weeks to assess progress; if good response, continue formula but reduce dose slightly to prevent overstimulation as qi regenerates. 4) If no response or worsening, consider secondary formula (Tian Wang Bu Xin Dan) or request repeat echocardiography to exclude structural disease (dilated cardiomyopathy, valvular dysfunction) not caught on initial screening. 5) After acute phase resolves, transition to a gentle tonification maintenance formula (e.g., Si Jun Zi Tang at lower dose) and continue stress reduction / rest protocols for 2–3 months to fully rebuild qi reserves and prevent recurrence.

The acute cardiac presentation in this patient requires immediate biomedical screening (ECG, cardiac enzyme panel, echocardiography) to exclude life-threatening conditions such as myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, heart failure, or pulmonary embolism. TCM herbal therapy and acupoint therapy should be pursued only after serious structural or acute pathology has been definitively ruled out by a physician. If at any point during treatment the patient experiences worsening dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, or other red-flag symptoms, TCM treatment should be halted and emergency medical evaluation sought immediately. This diagnosis is based on the limited examination data provided and does not substitute for a comprehensive in-person evaluation by a licensed TCM practitioner. The patient is responsible for disclosing all medications, supplements, and medical history to both their biomedical physician and TCM provider to ensure safe, coordinated care.
